Evolution of the male reproductive system in Penaeoidea (Dendrobranchiata): Integrating morphological and molecular data.
articles.authors: Fernanda C Salti, Marcos Tavares, Caio S Nogueira et al.
articles.abstract: Penaeoidea shrimps exhibit substantial diversity in reproductive morphology, but the evolutionary history of the male reproductive system (MRS) and its congruence with molecular phylogenies remain poorly understood. This study characterized MRS morphology across Penaeoidea and used these morphological data, together with a molecular phylogeny of the species analyzed herein, to reconstruct the ancestral states of MRS traits and investigate their evolutionary patterns and taxonomic implications. The MRS of 11 species was examined using histological methods, and phylogenetic analysis was conducted. In Benthesicymidae and Aristeidae, as well as in Solenoceridae and Penaeini, the median vas deferens (MVD) bears accessory and spermatic ducts, representing a synapomorphic trait and the putative plesiomorphic condition for Penaeoidea. In contrast, Trachypenaeini, Parapenaeini, and Sicyoniidae share a single duct in the MVD. Within Penaeini, the accessory gland is simple in Farfantepenaeus species but highly complex, with multiple glandular chambers, in Litopenaeus schmitti, supporting the separation of these lineages and arguing against treating Penaeus as a single genus. Benthesicymidae, Aristeidae, Solenoceridae, and Sicyoniidae lack accessory glands, representing a homoplastic condition, whereas Trachypenaeini and Parapenaeini exhibit a simplified accessory gland. The plesiomorphic spermatophore condition appears to be morphologically complex. Phylogenetic analyses recovered Penaeidae as paraphyletic, and substantial differences in MRS morphology among tribes support the hypothesis that these lineages may warrant elevation to family rank.

articles.title: Ad libitum eating and reduced exercise resolve impaired bone integrity after prolonged reductions in energy availability in mature female rodents.
articles.authors: Corinne E Metzger, Sibyl N Swift, Kyunghwa Baek et al.
articles.abstract: Reduced energy availability (EA) results in loss of bone mass and disruption of endocrine regulators of bone integrity, even in very active individuals. Our aim was to determine whether 12 weeks of less exercise and ad libitum eating would enable recovery of deficits incurred during 12 weeks of reduced EA, hypothesizing recovery would be improved in exercising rats. Female rats (n=64, 5 months old) were randomized to sedentary (SED) or exercise (EX) conditions and, within each group, to adlib-fed (ADLIB) or severe energy restriction (SEV-ER). Energy intake was restricted in all SEV-ER rats and exercise volume in SEV-ER EX rats calculated to produce equivalent 30% reductions in EA. After 12 weeks, SEV-ER EX rats exhibited no losses in lean/fat mass and total bone mass (DXA), metaphyseal %BV/TV, and distal femur and femoral neck vBMD (by pQCT), and higher values for osteoblast activity than observed in SEV-ER SED animals. EX did not protect against declines in serum leptin and IGF-I. Half of each group recovered for 12 weeks, eating ADLIB and (in EX rats) reducing running volume by 50%. After 4 weeks recovery, body weight and energy availability for all SEV-ER rats matched those of ADLIB rats. By 12 weeks, there were no significant differences among groups for all variables. These results demonstrate that bone mass/microarchitecture and osteoblast activity observed in SED animals can return to normal levels after a period of ad libitum eating, as can IGF-I/leptin in exercising rats with reduced exercise and ADLIB eating of the same duration as the preceding reduced EA.

articles.title: Hormone Replacement Therapy and Cerebral Hemodynamics in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.authors: Elyse Vetter, Keerti Vittalam, Sadie Winter et al.
articles.abstract: Background: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) has well-established effects on systemic vascular function in postmenopausal women, but its effects on cerebral hemodynamics remain poorly understood. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of HRT on ultrasound-based measures of cerebral hemodynamics. We hypothesized that HRT would be associated with reduced pulsatility index (PI), with stronger effects for estrogen-only formulations. Methods: Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched following PRISMA guidelines (January 25, 2026). Studies reporting PI, resistive index (RI), and cerebral blood velocity (CBV) in postmenopausal women using HRT were included. Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools. Multilevel meta-analytic models using restricted maximum likelihood accounted for dependency among effect sizes. Separate models examined between-group and within-individual comparisons. Moderator analyses examined hormone formulation and administration route. Results: Thirty-eight studies (27 meta-analyzed) were included. HRT was associated with lower PI versus controls, with a pooled mean difference of -0.051, 95% CI [-0.089, -0.012], p=0.009, k=31. Within-individual analyses demonstrated a reduction in PI over time, with a pooled mean change of -0.049, 95% CI [-0.081, -0.015], p=0.004, k=55. RI and CBV were not significantly altered (RI: p=0.74, CBV: p=0.54). Estrogen-only regimens were associated with greater reductions in PI than estrogen plus progestin or tibolone, while route of administration demonstrated no consistent effects. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial. Discussion: HRT was associated with reduced cerebrovascular pulsatility, suggesting a physiological effect on cerebral circulation. However, substantial heterogeneity across studies limits conclusions regarding factors that may modify this response.

articles.title: Maximum-Effort Jumping Exposes the Achilles Tendon to High Strain and Indicates Potential Overload in Adolescent Athletes.
articles.authors: Kolja Weidlich, Falk Mersmann, Theresa Domroes et al.
articles.abstract: Plyometric exercise is a fundamental component of many sport disciplines and may overload the Achilles tendon (AT) by subjecting it to high strain magnitudes. AT strain profiles were investigated during countermovement, drop, hurdle, and horizontal single-leg jumps - common plyometric exercises - in order to assess exercise-induced AT loading. This was done by measuring AT elongation during the jumps using reflective markers on the skin to reconstruct the AT path, while the myotendinous junction of the gastrocnemius medialis was recorded using ultrasound in 18 adolescent athletes. Electromyographic (EMG) activity of the tibialis anterior, soleus, gastrocnemius medialis and lateralis muscles, kinematics, and ground reaction forces were also measured. Although the maximum resultant ankle joint moment differed significantly between the investigated jumps, maximum AT strain and EMG activity of the triceps surae muscles were invariant between jump types. On average, the maximum AT strains ranged from 9.0% to 10.7%, and the EMG activity ranged from 0.96 to 1.43 times the maximum EMG activity achieved during a maximum voluntary fixed-end plantar flexion contraction, across the jumps. The consistently high AT strain magnitudes across the investigated jumps highlight the substantial mechanical demand placed on the AT during maximum-effort jumping tasks, which exceed the reported effective strain range for tendon adaptation. The frequent application of plyometric exercises involving such high-magnitude strains in training practice may contribute to AT overload in adolescent athletes.

articles.title: Characterising the plasma metabolome following high intensity interval exercise in continuous and intermittent hypoxia in overweight individuals.
articles.authors: Jacky Soo, Maartje Cox, Paul Goods et al.
articles.abstract: The aim of this work was to examine changes in the plasma metabolome in response to high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE) performed under three distinct hypoxia protocols. On separate days, 18 inactive individuals with overweight completed a HIIE protocol in randomised conditions: normoxia (NEx-NRec), normobaric hypoxia (inspired O2 fraction ∼0.14) during both the work and recovery (HEx-HRec), normobaric hypoxia during recovery only (NEx-HRec) and normobaric hypoxia during work only (HEx-NRec). Venous blood samples were collected before and after each HIIE for metabolite analyses by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry and 1H-nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Mean power output, averaged across the six work bouts, was lower in HEx-HRec compared to NEx-NRec, NEx-HRec and HEx-NRec (all P ≤ 0.009), with no differences (all P ≥ 0.11) between the other conditions. Arterial oxygen saturation was lower in HEx-HRec compared to other conditions (all P < 0.001). Concentrations of pyruvate and closely associated metabolites (alanine, citrate, lactate) increased consistently across all conditions (all P < 0.001; Hedge's g: 0.43-1.73), without differences between conditions (all P > 0.37). The lactate to pyruvate ratio increased in all conditions, but did not differ between them. Free-fatty acid (FFA) classes (saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated FFAs) showed consistent increases (all P < 0.001), while monounsaturated and saturated triacylglycerol (TAG) classes significantly decreased following HIIE (both P < 0.04). There were no condition × time interaction effects for any metabolites. HIIE significantly altered the concentration of glycolytic and TCA cycle intermediates, whilst concomitantly increasing FFA and decreasing TAG concentrations. Although hypoxia applied either continuously throughout HIIE or intermittently (work or recovery) during HIIE altered exercise performance and oxygen saturation, it had limited additional effect on metabolite concentrations.

articles.title: Changes in the Temporal Relationship Between Visual Information and Center of Pressure Displacements in Preterm Children: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.authors: Aline Aparecida Ribeiro, Rafael Nunes Briet, Ana Beatriz Oliver et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Premature children, even those without overt motor delays, may exhibit subtle impairments in sensory integration and visuomotor coordination. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to investigate the relationship between visual information and postural sway in preterm children at school age, under varying frequencies of visual stimulus provided by a moving room. DESIGN: This was a comparative cross-sectional study. SETTING: Children were assessed individually inside a "moving room" while standing on a force plate. PARTICIPANTS: Thirty-four children, aged 7.06 (0.75) years, were matched by age, gender, weight, and height. Seventeen were preterm (gestational age = 30.24 [3.56] weeks; birth weight = 1571 [568] g; 11 boys), and seventeen were full-term (gestational age = 39 [0.71] weeks; birth weight = 3250 [460] g; 11 boys). INTERVENTION(S) OR EXPOSURE(S): Children stood upright on a force plate inside the moving room, which oscillated in the anteroposterior direction at 2 frequencies (0.2 Hz and 0.5 Hz) with a constant peak velocity of 0.75 cm/s. MAIN OUTCOME(S) AND MEASURE(S): Measures of coupling between visual information and center of pressure (COP) displacements, including gain, phase and position variability, were calculated. Additionally, the magnitude of COP displacement was calculated across different visual conditions. RESULTS: Only preterm children showed a lower variability and a greater phase lag between visual information and COP displacements at 0.5 Hz compared to 0.2 Hz, relative to full-term children. COP mean amplitude was similar between groups across all conditions. CONCLUSIONS: Although COP displacements in preterm children were influenced by visual information similarly to full-term peers, their reduced variability and delayed postural responses at higher visual stimulus frequencies may indicate subtle alterations in visuomotor coupling. RELEVANCE: This pattern may compromise adequate sensorimotor tuning and reduce postural adaptation to challenging and dynamic visual environments.

articles.title: Target Trial Emulation: Considerations for Physical Therapy Research.
articles.authors: Kevin H McLaughlin, Kelly Daley, Amanda McQueen et al.
articles.abstract: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) are considered the ideal method for assessing the effectiveness of physical therapist interventions. However, RCTs are resource-intensive and usually take several years to complete, often providing insights well after they are needed to inform practice. Due to the constantly evolving nature of physical therapy, study designs are needed that can more rapidly generate evidence that can be used to guide clinical care. Target trial emulation (TTE) provides a framework that improves researchers' abilities to draw causal inferences from observational data, by specifying protocol components of a hypothetical RCT and emulating those components with observational data elements. By leveraging data generated through routine care encounters, TTE allows researchers to examine the effectiveness of interventions as they are being used in clinical care - enhancing researchers' abilities to generate evidence when it is most needed. However, TTE has not been used extensively among physical therapy researchers, potentially due to a lack of familiarity with this concept or challenges related to the way physical therapy is delivered or the types of data generated during physical therapist encounters. In this manuscript, the authors provide an introduction to the TTE framework, using an ongoing study examining the effectiveness of remote therapeutic monitoring as a case example. The authors also discuss considerations and challenges associated with TTE studies within the context of physical therapy and recommend strategies for addressing these challenges. They also discuss how TTE studies can be enhanced through the addition of implementation-focused data collection and conclude with a discussion of limitations associated with TTE studies.

articles.title: Good Science, Real Constraints: Ethics-Based Approaches to Managing Conflicting Incentives in Academic-Health System Research Partnerships.
articles.authors: Rachel A Prusynski, Kate I Minick, Michael P Johnson
articles.abstract: Partnerships between health systems and external academic researchers are increasingly central to embedded and learning health system (LHS) research in rehabilitation. Such partnerships offer substantial promise, but they also introduce ethical and practical challenges arising from conflicting incentives related to research rigor, timelines, dissemination, financial sustainability, and academic freedom. This perspective examines these challenges through the lens of the Ethics of Research and Implementation domain of the LHS Researcher Core Competencies, grounded in the ethical principles of the physical therapy profession. Drawing on existing literature and the authors' experience as academic-health system research partners, this perspective contrasts academic incentives (ie, grant funding, peer-reviewed publication, and generalizable knowledge) with health system incentives focused on operational efficiency, return on investment, and organizational reputation. Because health systems vary widely in their capacity to support research, this perspective presents a typology of partnership contexts and describes where ethical challenges may arise in each. This perspective then proposes ethics-based strategies for mutually beneficial research partnerships that apply across the different partnership contexts. These include transparent alignment of research goals with organizational priorities, accurate differentiation between research and quality improvement, attention to oversight particularly when a partner has less research infrastructure, pre-specification of outcomes, interim deliverables for health system stakeholders, and data use and publication agreements that protect academic freedom while allowing health system input. It illustrates these strategies with a partnership in which protected academic freedom and collaboration on dissemination allowed findings to reach national policy audiences. The Ethics of Research and Implementation competencies offer a practical framework for anticipating these conflicts and addressing them deliberately, enabling partnerships that generate rigorous knowledge while remaining useful to the health systems and patients they serve.

articles.title: Differential Postsurgery Outcomes Across Physical Therapy Care Pathways in Lumbar Spinal Stenosis Surgery: Analyses of a National Registry-Based Cohort.
articles.authors: Maria Fors, Birgitta Öberg, Paul Enthoven et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is the most common indication for spinal surgery. Physical therapist treatment is consistently recommended throughout the care pathway for LSS, including before and after surgical treatment. However, the effectiveness of pre- and postsurgery rehabilitation interventions are unclear. OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to explore 1-year postsurgery outcomes associated with different physical therapy care pathways in patients who had undergone surgery for LSS. DESIGN: This was a registry-based multicenter study using data from the Swedish National Spine Surgery Registry. SETTING: Swedish spine clinics participating in the Swedish National Spine Surgery Registry, with an estimated national coverage of 95%. PARTICIPANTS: Participants were patients surgically treated for LSS between 2021 and 2023 and with data on physical therapist treatment prior to a surgical decision, while waiting for surgery, and after surgery (N = 7969). INTERVENTION(S) OR EXPOSURE(S): Patient-reported exposure to physical therapy before and after LSS surgery, categorized into four physical therapy care pathways. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Outcomes were patient-reported pain intensity, disability, health-related quality of life, general health, gait function, analgesic use, repeat surgeries, satisfaction with surgery, and perceived participation in decision-making. Multivariable logistic regression and univariate analysis of variance were used to assess differences in 1-year postsurgery outcomes between 4 physical therapy care pathways. RESULTS: Compared to patients who reported pre- and postsurgery physical therapy, patients with only presurgery physical therapy demonstrated better outcomes across all measures and had higher odds of reaching the thresholds for meaningful and acceptable outcomes at 1 year after surgery (odds ratio [OR] = 1.39 to 1.56). In contrast, patients with only postsurgery physical therapy had higher pain intensity, worse gait function and health-related quality of life, and less improvement in disability and gait function. They also had lower odds of reaching clinically acceptable thresholds in pain intensity (spinal OR = 0.83 [96% CI = 0.74 to 0.93]; leg OR = 0.78 [95% CI = 0.67 to 0.88]) and disability (OR = 0.83 [95% CI = 0.72 to 0.96]). Few differences were observed between patients with both pre- and postsurgery physical therapy and those with no physical therapy. The latter group was small, and comparisons should be interpreted accordingly. CONCLUSIONS: Presurgery physical therapy may be beneficial to consider for patients undergoing surgery for LSS, while additional postsurgery physical therapy may not be warranted for all. RELEVANCE: The results may inform the development of surgical care pathways for LSS.
